title: Diagnostic Accuracy: Sensitivity, Specificity, Predictive Values and Likelihood Ratios
summary: Build a 2 × 2 table, calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV, show why predictive values depend on prevalence, and use likelihood ratios to convert pre-test to post-test probability.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 8 Hits 1, 3 and 5 (first lesson for Ch. 8). Checked against Trevethan 2017 and Deeks & Altman 2004 (read via page fetch); the worked prevalence example is arithmetic. Nuance: the reviewer states likelihood ratios are “NOT affected by prevalence”; Deeks & Altman describe them as allowing estimates that adapt for varying prior probabilities, and Trevethan notes all cell-based metrics depend on the sample. Not taught: ROC curves and AUC thresholds (Hit 6) — Altman & Bland 1994 notes were scanned and not readable; the explicit “lower cutoff raises sensitivity” direction (Hit 4).

objectives: Calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV from a 2 × 2 table.
Explain and quantify how prevalence changes predictive values.
Use likelihood ratios to convert pre-test to post-test probability.

scenes.title: A 99% test that is usually wrong
scenes.altText: An invented screening programme: a test with 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity is used on 1,000,000 people for a disease with prevalence 1 in 10,000. A patient tests positive and asks: “So I almost certainly have it?” Question token: “What is the chance a positive result is a true positive?”

cues.text: A test is 99 percent sensitive and 99 percent specific. It screens a million people for a disease that affects 1 in 10,000.
A patient tests positive and asks: so I almost certainly have it?
What is the real chance that a positive result is a true positive?

props.label: Chance a positive is truly positive?

scenes.title: The 2 × 2 table
scenes.altText: 2 × 2 card (Trevethan 2017): people are classified by a reference standard (disease present/absent) and by the test (positive/negative) into four cells: a = true positive, b = false positive, c = false negative, d = true negative. Formulas: sensitivity = a/(a + c); specificity = d/(b + d); positive predictive value (PPV) = a/(a + b); negative predictive value (NPV) = d/(c + d). Sensitivity uses only people WITH the condition; specificity only people WITHOUT it; PPV is the probability that a person with a positive test truly has the condition.

cues.text: Every test result falls into one of four cells. True positives, a; false positives, b; false negatives, c; and true negatives, d.
Sensitivity is a over a plus c: of the people who have the disease, the fraction the test calls positive. Specificity is d over b plus d: of those without it, the fraction called negative.
Positive predictive value is a over a plus b: of everyone who tests positive, the fraction who really have the disease. Negative predictive value is d over c plus d.
Notice the difference: sensitivity and specificity look down the disease columns; predictive values look across the test rows.

props.label: Sens/spec: by disease · PPV/NPV: by test result

scenes.title: Prevalence changes predictive value
scenes.altText: Worked example (arithmetic, 1,000,000 people, prevalence 1 in 10,000): diseased = 100 → true positives 99 (99% sensitivity), false negatives 1; healthy = 999,900 → false positives 9,999 (1% of healthy), true negatives 989,901. PPV = 99/(99 + 9,999) ≈ 1%; NPV ≈ 99.9999%. Same test at prevalence 10%: diseased 100,000 → TP 99,000; healthy 900,000 → FP 9,000; PPV = 99,000/108,000 ≈ 92%. Source token (Deeks & Altman 2004; Trevethan 2017): predictive values depend on the prevalence in the population tested and rarely generalize beyond it.

cues.text: Work it through for a million people. At 1 in 10,000, only 100 have the disease; the test finds 99 of them.
But 999,900 are healthy, and 1 percent of them, 9,999 people, test falsely positive.
So of 10,098 positives, only 99 are real. The positive predictive value is about 1 percent, despite a 99 percent test.
Use the same test where 10 percent have the disease, and the positive predictive value rises to about 92 percent.
Predictive values depend on prevalence in the population tested. Sensitivity and specificity did not change at all.

scenes.title: Likelihood ratios and post-test probability
scenes.altText: LR card (Deeks & Altman 2004): LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity. Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR; probability = odds/(1 + odds). LRs allow probability estimates while adapting for varying prior probabilities. Worked: 99%/99% test → LR+ = 0.99/0.01 = 99. Pre-test probability 1/10,000 → odds ≈ 0.0001 → post-test odds ≈ 0.0099 → probability ≈ 1% (matches the table). Deeks example: pre-test 0.1 → odds 0.11; LR ≈ 20.4 → post-test odds 2.27 → probability ≈ 0.69. Trade-off token (Trevethan 2017): cell values depend on how stringent the test cutoff is; there are trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity. Back to the hook: “about a 1% chance” — confirm with a more specific test.

cues.text: Likelihood ratios combine sensitivity and specificity. The positive likelihood ratio is sensitivity divided by one minus specificity; the negative is one minus sensitivity divided by specificity.
To use one, convert the pre-test probability to odds, multiply by the likelihood ratio, then convert the post-test odds back to a probability.
For our 99 percent test, LR-positive is 99. Starting odds of about 1 in 10,000 become about 1 in 100: roughly a 1 percent chance, the same answer as the table.
Results also depend on how stringent the cut-off is: there are trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity.
Back to the patient: a positive result means about a 1 percent chance of disease. Confirm it with a more specific test.

props.label: Hook: ≈ 1% chance → confirm with a specific test

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “99% sensitive and specific means a positive is 99% likely true” (✓ PPV depends on prevalence — ≈ 1% at 1 in 10,000); “Sensitivity changes with prevalence” (✓ sensitivity/specificity are computed within disease groups; predictive values change with prevalence); “PPV = a/(a + c)” (✓ that is sensitivity; PPV = a/(a + b)).

cues.text: Trap one: a 99 percent sensitive and specific test means a positive is 99 percent likely to be true. No: positive predictive value depends on prevalence, and here it is about 1 percent.
Trap two: sensitivity changes with prevalence. Sensitivity and specificity are computed within the disease groups; it is the predictive values that move with prevalence.
Trap three: PPV is a over a plus c. That is sensitivity. PPV is a over a plus b, true positives over all positives.

props.title: ✗ “PPV = a/(a + c).”
lines: ✓ That is sensitivity; PPV = a/(a + b)

scenes.title: Columns vs rows
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Sens and spec live in the DISEASE columns; PPV and NPV live in the TEST rows — and rows move when prevalence moves.” Tokens: Sens = a/(a+c) · Spec = d/(b+d) · PPV = a/(a+b) · NPV = d/(c+d). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: sensitivity and specificity live in the disease columns; predictive values live in the test rows, and the rows move whenever prevalence moves.

Where it breaks: sensitivity and specificity can also differ between populations with different disease severity or spectrum; the cut-off chosen changes them; and the table layout varies between textbooks, so check which cell is which.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Sens = a/(a+c) · Spec = d/(b+d) · PPV = a/(a+b) · NPV = d/(c+d)”, “PPV/NPV depend on prevalence (99%/99% at 1 in 10,000 → PPV ≈ 1%) · LR+ = sens/(1−spec) · post-odds = pre-odds × LR”.

cues.text: Sensitivity and specificity describe the test within diseased and healthy groups, but predictive values depend on prevalence, so even a 99 percent test gives a positive predictive value near 1 percent for a disease affecting 1 in 10,000.

props.label: Sens a/(a+c) · Spec d/(b+d) · PPV a/(a+b) · NPV d/(c+d)
PPV depends on prevalence · LR+ = sens/(1−spec) · post-odds = pre-odds × LR

explanation.what: Plain language: sensitivity is how well a test finds people who have a disease, specificity how well it clears people who don’t, and predictive values answer the patient’s question — “given my result, what is my chance?” — which depends on how common the disease is. Scientific terms: 2 × 2 table, true/false positive/negative, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, prevalence (pre-test probability), likelihood ratio, odds, post-test probability.
explanation.why: Sensitivity and specificity are calculated within the diseased and non-diseased groups separately. Predictive values mix the two groups, so when disease is rare, even a small false-positive rate among many healthy people swamps the true positives.
explanation.measure: Sensitivity = a/(a + c); specificity = d/(b + d); PPV = a/(a + b); NPV = d/(c + d) (Trevethan 2017). LR+ = sens/(1 − spec); LR− = (1 − sens)/spec; post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR; probability = odds/(1 + odds) (Deeks & Altman 2004). Worked: 99%/99% at 1 in 10,000 → PPV ≈ 1%; at 10% → ≈ 92%.
explanation.differs: Sensitivity/specificity (properties within disease groups) vs predictive values (depend on prevalence); LR+ (rule in) vs LR− (rule out).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate a metric from a 2 × 2 table, explain a low PPV in screening, and convert pre-test probability with a likelihood ratio.

questions.stem: In a study, 90 of 100 diseased people test positive and 160 of 200 non-diseased people test negative. What are the sensitivity and specificity?

options.rationale: Incorrect. 20% is the false-positive rate (1 − specificity).
Incorrect. These mix in predictive-value denominators.

questions.stem: Using the same study (90 TP, 10 FN, 40 FP, 160 TN), what is the positive predictive value?

options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the negative predictive value.

questions.stem: A test with fixed sensitivity and specificity is moved from a specialist clinic (high prevalence) to population screening (low prevalence). What happens?

options.rationale: Correct. Predictive values depend on prevalence; rarer disease means more false positives relative to true positives.
Incorrect. Sensitivity is calculated within diseased people and does not depend on prevalence in this way.
Incorrect. Predictive values change with prevalence.

Predictive values depend on prevalence; worked example (arithmetic).
Likelihood ratio formulas and odds conversion.
ROC curves and AUC thresholds; explicit cut-off direction (lower cut-off → higher sensitivity); LRs “not affected by prevalence”; spectrum effects.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer says likelihood ratios are “NOT affected by prevalence”. Deeks & Altman 2004 present LRs as adapting to varying prior probabilities; like sensitivity and specificity, they can still vary with disease spectrum between populations.
